title: Quantity Words for Countable and Uncountable Things
goal: Choose common Norwegian quantity words for countable things, amounts, all, whole, and both.

objectives.statement: Choose common Norwegian quantity words for countable things, amounts, all, whole, and both.

spans.value: Sara and Jonas are preparing dinner at Sara’s flat. Two neighbours are coming with their children, so Sara checks what they already have before going to the shop.
Seks. Begge naboene kommer, og alle barna deres blir med.

blocks.translation: Six. Both neighbours are coming, and all their children are coming too.

spans.value: Vi har mye ris og noen tomater, men lite melk og få gulrøtter.

blocks.translation: We have plenty of rice and some tomatoes, but little milk and few carrots.

spans.value: Da kjøper jeg litt melk og noen gulrøtter.

blocks.translation: Then I’ll buy some milk and some carrots.

spans.value: Flott. Jeg lager mat hele ettermiddagen.
Da blir alt klart før klokka seks.

blocks.translation: Then everything will be ready before six o’clock.

spans.value: The quantity words help Sara and Jonas answer several different questions:

items.value: Can the things be counted individually?
Are they talking about an amount instead?
Do they mean every member of a group?
Do they mean one complete thing or period?
Is the group made up of exactly two members?

spans.value: Norwegian uses different words for these meanings. English sometimes hides the difference by using words such as some or all in several situations.

sections.title: Things you count and amounts you measure

spans.value: refers to things you can normally count individually:

no.value: én tomat, to tomater, tre tomater

en.value: one tomato, two tomatoes, three tomatoes

spans.value: is normally treated as an amount rather than as separate units:
You can count packets of rice or glasses of milk, but rice and milk themselves are normally treated as amounts. This distinction controls several common quantity words.

sections.title: Many or much: mange and mye

en.value: We have a lot of rice.
She drinks a lot of coffee.

spans.value: The same distinction appears in questions:

en.value: How much milk do we need?

items.value: mange + plural things you can count
mye + an amount you do not normally count directly

no.value: Hvor mange kopper kaffe lager du?

en.value: How many cups of coffee are you making?
How much coffee are you making?

spans.value: In the first question, the cups are counted. In the second, coffee is treated as an amount.

A common mistake is to choose according to the noun’s physical nature alone. The intended unit matters. Coffee is usually an amount, but cups of coffee are countable. Similarly, bread can be an amount, while loaves or slices are countable.
One useful exception to notice is
, money. Although the Norwegian noun has a plural form, it is normally treated as an amount:

en.value: They have a lot of money.

spans.value: When the exact quantity is not important, Norwegian commonly uses

no.value: Det er noe ris i skapet.

en.value: There is some rice in the cupboard.
Do you have a little time?

spans.value: emphasizes a small amount, often in a neutral or useful way.

en.value: Can you buy a little bread?

spans.value: Both can be natural. The first asks for an unspecified amount. The second presents the requested amount as small.
Questions often preserve the same count-and-amount distinction:
directly with an ordinary plural countable noun in this meaning.

sections.title: Few and little: få, lite and litt

spans.value: with plural countable nouns when the number is small.
with uncountable nouns when the amount is small.
often suggest that the quantity is smaller than wanted or expected. That implication matters.
This can suggest pressure: there may not be enough time.
often presents the small amount more neutrally or positively:
Here the speaker emphasizes that some time is available.
A similar contrast is possible with countable nouns:
The first emphasizes the low number. The second presents a small number of guests without necessarily making it sound like a failure.

no.value: Vi har lite melk, så Sara må kjøpe mer.

en.value: We have little milk, so Sara has to buy more.

no.value: Vi har litt melk til kaffen.

en.value: We have a little milk for the coffee.

spans.value: The amount may be small in both cases. The speaker’s view of that amount differs.

sections.title: All members of a group: all, alt and alle

spans.value: Norwegian changes the word corresponding to English all according to the noun.

en.value: All the chairs are around the table.

spans.value: with a singular common-gender noun, especially an amount:
can also stand alone and mean everything:
For a specific plural group, Norwegian commonly uses
followed by the definite plural noun:
A common mistake is to use
before every noun because it can mean everything. Its form still has to fit its job.

en.value: All the sugar is on the table.

sections.title: Every member or one complete thing?

spans.value: English all can describe every member of a group or one complete thing. Norwegian normally distinguishes these ideas.
for every member of a plural group:
for one complete thing, person, group treated as a unit, or period of time. The noun normally has definite form.

no.value: Jonas brukte hele ettermiddagen på maten.

en.value: Jonas spent the whole afternoon on the food.

spans.value: The contrast becomes clear when number changes:
In the first sentence, several complete members of a group are included. In the second, one book is considered from beginning to end.
The first focuses on the full available amount. The second treats the bread as one complete item.
for all day. A day is one complete period, so Norwegian uses:
when all members of a group are included and that group contains exactly two.
can also stand alone when the two people or things are already known:

no.value: Vil Sara og Jonas ha kaffe? Begge vil ha kaffe.

en.value: Do Sara and Jonas want coffee? Both want coffee.

spans.value: only when there are two. Use
when every member of a larger or unspecified group is included.
A common error is to use
simply because every person is included. The size of the group matters.

no.value: Begge foreldrene mine bor i Bergen.

en.value: Both my parents live in Bergen.

no.value: Alle vennene mine bor i Bergen.

en.value: All my friends live in Bergen.

spans.value: Dinner is almost ready. Sara returns from the shop.
Nå har vi mye melk og mange gulrøtter.

Good. All the guests have arrived.

Have they used all the glasses?

blocks.translation: Almost. There are some glasses left in the kitchen.

spans.value: Now change the situation. Two friends are packing for a weekend at a cabin. They have several bags, an amount of food and water, two maps, one whole weekend and a list of jobs that must all be completed.

prompt.value: Sort each Norwegian noun into the group for individual countable items or the group for uncountable amounts. Treat each noun as used in the dinner scene.

explanation.value: Countable plural nouns select forms such as mange, noen, få, and alle; mass or uncountable nouns select mye, noe, lite, and alt.

prompt.value: Complete each Norwegian note or question with noen, noe, or litt. Use the noun and the context to decide whether the amount is unspecified or deliberately small.

explanation.value: Use noen with countable plurals, noe with an unspecified amount, and litt for a small amount.

prompt.value: Complete each Norwegian description with få or lite. Use få with a small number of plural countable things and lite with a small amount.

explanation.value: Få modifies plural countable nouns; lite modifies an uncountable amount.

prompt.value: Choose the option that matches both situations. Situation 1 describes a small amount that is available and enough. Situation 2 describes a small amount that is insufficient and requires buying more.

options.text: 1) Vi har lite melk til kaffen; det er nok. 2) Vi har litt melk; det er ikke nok, så vi må kjøpe mer.
options.why: The forms are reversed for the sufficient and insufficient situations.

options.text: 1) Vi har litt melk til kaffen; det er nok. 2) Vi har lite melk; det er ikke nok, så vi må kjøpe mer.
options.why: Litt presents a small available amount neutrally; lite presents an insufficient amount.

stem.value: Which option uses litt and lite with the intended meanings?

prompt.value: Complete each Norwegian sentence with all, alt, or alle. Use the noun or the independent meaning everything as evidence.

explanation.value: Alle agrees with plural nouns, alt with neuter singular or the meaning everything, and all with common-gender singular.

prompt.value: Choose the option whose quantity words match both cleaning situations. Situation 1 concerns every member of a plural group. Situation 2 concerns one kitchen cleaned as one complete whole.

options.text: 1) Sara vasket alle glassene. 2) Sara vasket hele kjøkkenet.
options.why: Alle marks every member of the plural group; hele marks one complete kitchen.

explanation.value: Begge means exactly two members; alle refers to the complete group when it can contain more than two.

prompt.value: Write a short connected exchange in Norwegian between two friends packing for a weekend at a cabin. Write 10–14 sentences and use each taught form at least once: mange, mye, noen, noe, litt, få, lite, all, alt, alle, hele, and begge. Make the cabin context show a clear reason for each choice: plural countable items, uncountable amounts, an unspecified amount, a small amount, a small insufficient number, a small insufficient amount, every member of a plural group, all of a common-gender amount, everything, one complete weekend, and both members of an exactly-two group.

payload.judge_prompt: Check the response against the cabin task and report evidence for each criterion. Accept natural Bokmål wording and sentence order when the required quantity meanings and listed forms remain clear.

criteria.instruction: Uses each of mange, mye, noen, noe, litt, få, lite, all, alt, alle, hele, and begge naturally and matches each form to its intended noun or meaning.
Makes countability, amount, group scope, whole-period, and exactly-two meanings clear in the connected cabin exchange.

prompt.value: Write eight short Norwegian sentences in a new household context, one for each meaning: many countable items, much of an amount, some countable items, a small insufficient amount, every member of a group, one complete period, everything, and both members of an exactly-two group. Make each context clear.

payload.judge_prompt: Check the eight sentences against the task and report evidence for each criterion. Accept natural Bokmål nouns and phrasing when the requested quantity meaning is clear; do not require exact sentence wording.

criteria.instruction: Uses mange with a plural countable household noun to express many countable items.
Uses mye with an uncountable household amount.
Uses noen with plural countable household items to express some.
Uses lite with an uncountable amount and makes its insufficiency clear.
Uses alle with a plural group to express every member.
Uses hele with a definite period to express one complete period.
Uses alt independently to express everything.
Uses begge for the members of an explicitly exactly-two group.
